701.title: The prince's unease
701.hook: the road cleared of the old and sick, yet the gods place an old man in his path (Buddhacarita 3)
701.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers return to the sights of old age, sickness and death when teaching impermanence, and the scenes are painted on temple walls and told to children in Buddhist communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, life in the palace, and your line: a father's fear. Did you find the love inside someone's grip? Today the prince asks to go outside. Day seven hundred one.

Orders go out across the city. Sweep the royal road. Hang garlands. Set out banners and flowers. And one more order, the strange one: anyone old, anyone sick, anyone suffering, keep them off the road today. The prince has heard about the gardens outside the walls and asked to see them, and the king has said yes, on one condition. The world his son sees will be a world with the hard parts taken out. By the time the chariot rolls through the gate, the street is perfect. Faces at every window. Not a single bent back in sight.
screen: `SWEEP THE ROAD. HANG GARLANDS.` → `KEEP THE OLD AND SICK AWAY.` → `A PERFECT STREET.`

segments.voice: First, the crowd. The poem spends time on the city's excitement. People hurry to rooftops and windows to catch sight of the prince going by, and they look at him with delight. It's a parade. And for a moment the king's plan seems to work. Second, the gap. The road has been cleared. Nobody old should be there. So the poem says the gods of the pure abodes made one: an old man appears in the prince's path, bent over, white-haired, leaning on a stick. The wall the king built was solid. Something came through it anyway. Third, the question. The prince turns to his charioteer and asks what this is. A man who looks like that, what happened to him? The charioteer answers simply: this is old age. It takes beauty and strength and memory. This man was a child once, and grew, and this is where the years have brought him. Then the question that matters. Will this happen to me? The answer is yes. To you, and to everyone. Fourth, the unease. In the poem the prince is shaken to the core. He can't enjoy the gardens. He asks to turn back. So here's the turn the poem is making. The king's whole plan was about keeping things out. The poem's answer is that some truths don't need permission. The road was cleared, and it got through.
screen: `A CITY AT ITS WINDOWS.` · `THE GODS PLACE AN OLD MAN.` · `WILL THIS HAPPEN TO ME?` · `SOME TRUTHS DON'T NEED PERMISSION.` · then, large: `IT GETS THROUGH ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at your own hands. Settle, and breathe. Turn your hands over slowly and look at them as if for the first time. The lines at the knuckles. The creases of the palm. Any scar, any spot. These hands were small once. They will change again. Ask the prince's question quietly, without fear: will this happen to me? Let the honest answer be there, and keep breathing beside it. The bell holds the time.
The prince's unease. On a road cleared of every hard sight, an old man appears, and the prince learns that age will come to him too. Today's word.
Your line: it gets through anyway. Today, when a hard truth slips past your defenses, let it finish speaking before you turn the chariot around. Day seven hundred one.

screen: `DAY 701 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SICK AND THE DEAD.`

702.title: The sick and the dead
702.hook: the prince asks the charioteer, and the world goes gray (Buddhacarita 3)
702.howItsDone: Some Buddhists, especially in monastic settings, reflect regularly on sickness, aging and death as part of practice, and Buddhist funerals can include chanting on impermanence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prince's unease, and your line: it gets through anyway. Did a hard truth slip past your defenses, and did you let it finish speaking? Day seven hundred two.

Who is that man? A question a child might ask from the back seat of a car. The prince keeps asking it in this canto, and each answer takes something away. First, a man by the road with a swollen belly, breathing hard, leaning on others, crying out. Then a group of men carrying something on a frame, wrapped in cloth, with people walking behind them weeping. The palace wall has already cracked once. Now the poem widens the crack, one honest answer at a time.
screen: `WHO IS THAT MAN?` → `A SICK MAN BY THE ROAD.` → `A BODY CARRIED, PEOPLE WEEPING.`

segments.voice: First, sickness. The charioteer explains: this man is ill. Something in his body has gone wrong, and it has brought him low. Can it happen to anyone? Yes. The poem has the prince shaken again, looking at the crowds on the road and wondering how they can be cheerful with this so close. Second, death. The body on the frame. The poem says the gods moved the charioteer to tell the truth, even though the king would rather he didn't. This man has died, he says. He is like a log now. His family carried him out and they are weeping. And the prince asks the last question. Is this the end for everyone? It is, the charioteer says. High or low, it comes to all. Third, the gray. Now the prince looks around, and the poem shows the change in him. The same crowds, the same banners, the same gardens. Nothing outside has moved. But the color has drained out of it for him. He wonders aloud how people can go about laughing and careless when death is certain and close. That astonishment has an echo in the Dhammapada. In Max Müller's translation: "How is there laughter, how is there joy, as this world is always burning?" And fourth, where it leaves him. Sunk, you might expect. But he keeps asking, and the question has turned outward: how can a whole street laugh beside this? That puzzle about other people, more than his own sadness, is what the next cantos follow. The garden, a friend's advice, and the night ride out of the city all grow from it.
screen: `SICKNESS: CAN IT HAPPEN TO ANYONE?` · `DEATH: IS THIS THE END FOR EVERYONE?` · `NOTHING MOVED, BUT THE COLOR WENT.` · `HE KEEPS ASKING.` · then, large: `THE WORLD GOES GRAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one hard fact, kindly. Settle, and breathe. Choose one true thing you'd usually rather not think about. Someone you love will get sick one day. This body will age. A day will come that's your last. Pick just one, and say it to yourself plainly. Then, instead of pushing it away, put a hand on your chest, or soften your shoulders, and hold the fact the way you'd hold a frightened friend's hand. Not fixing. Just holding. When your mind runs off, come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
The sick and the dead. The second and third sights in the poem, a sick man and a body carried with mourners, and the prince's question: is this for everyone? Today's word.
screen: `THE SICK AND THE DEAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the world goes gray. If something today drains the color out of an ordinary moment, don't rush the color back. Stay with it for one breath before you move on. Day seven hundred two.

screen: `DAY 702 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WOMEN IN THE GARDEN.`

703.title: The women in the garden
703.hook: the women are sent to charm him, and he stays unmoved (Buddhacarita 4)
703.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers use the garden scene when speaking about sense pleasures and restraint, and in temple murals the prince is sometimes shown seated calmly among dancers and musicians.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sick and the dead, and your line: the world goes gray. Did you stay a breath longer with something hard? Today the king tries one more remedy. Day seven hundred three.

The king has heard. His son came home from the road shaken, and now he won't stop thinking about old age and death. So the king reaches for the tool he trusts. He sends the prince to a beautiful garden outside the city, and he sends the women of the court with him. Their task is plain: delight him. Bring him back to the life of pleasure. Make him forget what he saw. Music under the trees. Flowers. Laughter by the water. The poem spends a long time in this garden, and every line of it is built to pull a young man's attention away from one thought.
screen: `THE KING TRIES AGAIN.` → `A GARDEN, MUSIC, THE COURT'S WOMEN.` → `MAKE HIM FORGET.`

segments.voice: First, the women. It matters how the poem sets this up. They didn't choose this. They were sent, by a king, with a task. At first, the poem says, they hold back, shy before the prince. Then they're urged on, and they do what they were told. They sing and dance, they tease and whisper, they wander close in the flowering garden. The poet describes it all at length, with the color and play of court poetry. Second, the prince. He doesn't scold them. He doesn't run. In the poem he simply isn't moved. He looks at the young women, bright and laughing, and what he sees is what the road just taught him: this beauty will age, these bodies will sicken, these lives will end. He's not cold toward them. He's thinking about them more truly than the garden wants him to. Third, the word itself. Unmoved doesn't mean frozen, or proud, or disgusted. In the Anguttara Nikaya the Buddha names eight worldly conditions, gain and loss, good name and bad name, praise and blame, pleasure and pain, and describes a mind they don't overturn. In the garden only the pleasant half is pulling, and steadiness looks like quiet. And fourth, the cost to the king. Another remedy has failed. The music played, the garden bloomed, and his son came home thinking the same thought. The poem doesn't blame anyone in the garden. The women did what they were asked. The prince did what he couldn't help. And the garden isn't finished with him yet. Before he goes home, a friend will try.
screen: `SENT, NOT CHOOSING.` · `HE SEES WHAT THE ROAD TAUGHT HIM.` · `UNMOVED IS NOT COLD.` · `THE KING'S REMEDY FAILS.` · then, large: `UNMOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one charm you can resist. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that pulls at you during an ordinary day. The phone face-down on the table. A snack you're not hungry for. A show that starts the next episode on its own. Pick one, and picture it in front of you now. Feel the pull, honestly, without pretending it isn't there. Then breathe, and let the pull rise and pass without obeying it. You're not fighting it. You're just not moved. The bell holds the time.
The women in the garden. Sent by the king to charm the prince back to pleasure, they find him courteous and unmoved, thinking of age and death. Today's word.
screen: `THE WOMEN IN THE GARDEN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: unmoved. Once today, when something built to grab you starts pulling, take one breath first, and see if you can stay upright and kind at the same time. Day seven hundred three.

what a scholar hears: the canto is written with the lush detail of court poetry, so the reader feels the pull the prince is resisting.

704.title: Udayin's advice
704.hook: a friend urges him to enjoy life while he's young; the prince answers about aging (Buddhacarita 4)
704.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers describe sense pleasures as impermanent rather than evil in themselves, and this conversation can be retold as an example of disagreeing with kindness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the women in the garden, and your line: unmoved. Did you take one breath before something pulled you? Today, still in the garden, a friend speaks up. Day seven hundred four.

Look, I'm saying this because I care. A friend takes you aside and goes on: you're too serious. Relax. You've got your whole life for the heavy stuff. In the garden, that friend is Udayin, the son of the king's priest, a young man the prince knows well. He has watched the women try and fail. So he goes to the prince himself, and makes the case for pleasure. It's a good case. The poem lets him make it fully, and that's what makes the prince's answer worth hearing.
screen: `THE FRIEND WHO TAKES YOU ASIDE.` → `UDAYIN, THE PRIEST'S SON.` → `THE CASE FOR PLEASURE.`

segments.voice: First, the argument. Udayin speaks as a friend, frankly. Even if your heart isn't in it, he says, be courteous to these women; turning away from them is unkind. Then he reaches for old stories: great sages of the past, he says, were won over by love and pleasure, so why should you hold out? And his last point is the one friends still make: enjoy these things now, while you're young. There's time later for the forest. Second, how the prince listens. He lets Udayin finish, all of it, the courtesy, the old stories, the advice about youth. When he answers, he starts by granting what's true in it. Third, the answer. In the poem, paraphrased here, the prince says: I don't despise the pleasures of the world. I know people are bound up in them. But I keep remembering that it all passes. Age is coming, and sickness, and death. If those three weren't real, I too would find delight here. Because they are, my heart can't settle into it. That's the whole reply. Not that pleasure is wicked. That it doesn't last, and he has seen that, and he can't unsee it. Fourth, the tone. In the poem he answers without contempt. He even turns the friend's advice around: if Udayin is truly his friend, he asks, why urge him toward what will end, instead of helping him find what won't? A disagreement between friends, with no one stomping off. And the king's plan fails again. A good argument, kindly heard, kindly declined.
screen: `ENJOY IT WHILE YOU'RE YOUNG.` · `HE TAKES THE ARGUMENT SERIOUSLY.` · `NOT WICKED. IT JUST DOESN'T LAST.` · `A DISAGREEMENT BETWEEN FRIENDS.` · then, large: `HE ANSWERED GENTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear out one worldly argument. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a voice, a friend's, a relative's, your own, that says something like: why so serious? Have fun. Get ahead. You only live once. Let it make its case in your head, fully, without interrupting. Notice what's true in it. Then, if you have an answer, let it come, the way the prince's did: without contempt, without a speech. Just: I hear you, and here's what I keep remembering. The bell holds the time.
Udayin's advice. A friend urges the prince to enjoy pleasure while he's young; the prince answers that it all passes, and he can't forget it. Today's word.
Your line: he answered gently. Today, when you disagree with someone who means well, find the true thing in what they said, say it back, and then answer. Day seven hundred four.

705.title: The plowed field
705.hook: he sees worms turned up by the plow and feels grief for them; then meets a wanderer (Buddhacarita 5)
705.howItsDone: Care for small creatures runs through Buddhist practice: the first precept is to refrain from taking life, and in some monastic traditions monks strain their drinking water or take care where they walk to avoid harming insects.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Udayin's advice, and your line: he answered gently. Did you find the true thing in a well-meant argument? Today the prince rides out past the city, into the fields. Day seven hundred five.

Fresh soil, turned over in long rows. If you've ever dug a garden bed, you've seen what comes up with it: worms, grubs, beetles, small things suddenly in the open air, some of them cut in half by the blade. It's easy to step over them without a thought. The prince, riding out toward the forest, stops his horse at the edge of a plowed field and looks. And the poem says what he feels. Not disgust. Not curiosity. Grief, the kind a person feels for family.
screen: `FRESH SOIL, TURNED OVER.` → `SMALL LIVES IN THE OPEN AIR.` → `HE STOPS AND LOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, the field. In the poem, the ground has been torn by the plow, the young grass ripped up, and the earth is strewn with tiny creatures, insects and worms, killed or dying. The prince sees them, and grieves, the poem says, as if his own kin had been slain. Second, the people. His grief doesn't stop at the worms. He sees the plowmen too, their bodies darkened by wind and sun and dust, and the oxen worn out from dragging the plow. The same look of mercy falls on all of them. Small creatures, tired men, tired animals. Nobody in the field is the villain. Everyone in it is suffering something. Third, the stillness. He gets down from his horse and walks, sorrowful, and sits beneath a rose-apple tree. There he thinks about birth and death in the world, and his mind grows quiet and clear. The poem describes him settling into the first stage of deep meditation, right there at the edge of a working field. And fourth, the visitor. A figure in a wanderer's robe comes toward him, someone the poem says no one else can see. The prince asks who he is. The wanderer answers that he has left home, afraid of birth and death, to seek freedom. Then, the poem says, he rises into the sky and is gone. He was a god in disguise, come to show the prince the road. Here the poem joins the field and the fourth sight into one scene. The grief comes first. The calm under the tree comes next. And only then does the wanderer appear, as if the prince had to feel for the smallest lives before he could see the way out for all of them.
screen: `WORMS IN THE TURNED SOIL.` · `PLOWMEN AND OXEN, TOO.` · `CALM UNDER THE ROSE-APPLE TREE.` · `A WANDERER, THEN GONE.` · then, large: `GRIEF FOR THE SMALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice small lives underfoot. If you can, look at the ground near you, a floor, a lawn, a crack in the pavement, a windowsill. If you can't, close your eyes and bring one to mind. Look for something tiny that's alive: an ant, a spider, a moss, a weed pushing up. Watch it for a while. Let it be as real to you as a person would be. No need to rescue it or name it. Just give it your full attention, the way the prince did at the edge of the field. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The plowed field. Worms turned up by the plow, tired men and oxen, grief as for family, then calm under a tree, and a wanderer who shows the way. Today's word.
Your line: grief for the small. Today, before you step, sweep or spray, look down once, and let one small life be real to you. Day seven hundred five.

706.title: The flight
706.hook: the palace asleep, the gates opening, the horse's hooves muffled (Buddhacarita 5)
706.howItsDone: The prince's leaving, often called the great going forth, is remembered in Buddhist art and at festivals, and in Theravada countries young men about to ordain sometimes ride in procession on a horse or are carried, recalling the prince's ride out of the city.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plowed field, and your line: grief for the small. Did you look down once and let a small life be real? Today, night falls on the palace. Day seven hundred six.

Before he leaves, he asks. That's the part of the flight that's easy to forget. The prince comes back from the field and goes to his father, bows, and says it out loud: let me go and become a wanderer. The king weeps. Not yet, he says. You're young. Wait. Then the prince makes an offer. Promise me four things, and I'll stay: that my life won't end in death, that sickness won't take my health, that age won't take my youth, that misfortune won't take what I have. The king can't promise any of them. Nobody could. And so the asking ends, and the night begins.
screen: `FIRST, HE ASKS.` → `PROMISE ME FOUR THINGS.` → `NO ONE COULD.`

segments.voice: First, the sleeping palace. Back in his rooms, the women play music for him as always, but the poem says the gods send a heavy sleep over them, and they fall where they are, instruments still in their arms. Year one stood in that room. Tonight the poem only passes through it on the way to the door. Second, the horse. The prince wakes Chandaka, his attendant, and asks for Kanthaka, his horse. And Chandaka brings him. The prince speaks to the horse as to a friend, asking him to carry him well this one time. Third, the gates. All his life this palace has been a machine for keeping the prince in and the world out. Heavy doors. Bars. Guards. And tonight, the poem says, the gates that took strength to move swing open by themselves, without a sound. The city sleeps on. Fourth, the look back. Outside the city, the poem has the prince turn toward it and make a vow: he won't come back into this city until he has seen the far shore of birth and death. Then he rides on into the dark. Here's the arc of the last days. A father built walls. A cleared road, a garden, a friend's advice, a palace full of music. One by one, they gave. Tonight, the last one does. The gates open.
screen: `THE PALACE FALLS ASLEEP.` · `CHANDAKA BRINGS THE HORSE.` · `HEAVY GATES, OPENING ALONE.` · `A VOW TO THE FAR SHORE.` · then, large: `THE GATES OPEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: move quietly for a minute. Stand if you can, or stay seated and move just your hands. Then move as if everyone in the house were asleep. Slow. Soft. Set each foot down so it makes no sound. Lift a cup and set it down without a click. Notice how much attention quiet takes, and how the room seems to get bigger when you stop making noise in it. When the minute's done, sit, and rest in the hush you made. The bell holds the time.
The flight. The prince asks his father first, is refused, then leaves at night on Kanthaka with Chandaka, through gates that open on their own. Today's word.
Your line: the gates open. Today, notice one door you've been waiting on, and ask whether you've said out loud what you need. Day seven hundred six.

707.title: Chandaka sent back
707.hook: the charioteer begs to stay; the prince sends him home with his jewels (Buddhacarita 6)
707.howItsDone: The cutting of the hair and the change into a plain robe are remembered in Buddhist ordinations, where in some communities a new monk or nun has the head shaved and puts on the robe before taking vows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flight, and your line: the gates open. Did you say out loud what you need? Today the night ride ends at the edge of a forest. Day seven hundred seven.

Sunrise, and a horse that has run all night stands blowing at the edge of a hermitage. A young man climbs down. For the first time in his life, there is no palace behind him. Beside him stands Chandaka, the attendant who saddled the horse in the dark and rode out with him. He has done everything he was told all night. Now the prince gives him one more order: go home. And Chandaka says no.
screen: `SUNRISE AT THE HERMITAGE.` → `ONE MORE ORDER: GO HOME.` → `CHANDAKA SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: First, the thanks. Before any parting, the prince praises Chandaka. In the poem he says, in paraphrase, that this loyalty is rare: a man who follows his master when there is nothing to gain by it. The thank-you comes first. Second, the jewels. The prince takes off his ornaments and puts them in Chandaka's hands, with a message for the king. Tell my father, he says, that I haven't gone into the forest out of anger, or for lack of love, or out of longing for heaven. I've gone to put an end to old age and death. Don't grieve for me. Third, the begging. Chandaka weeps. How can I lead this horse home with an empty saddle? What do I say to your father, to the queen who raised you, to your wife? Don't send me back. The prince answers gently, with an image from the poem: beings meet the way birds gather in one tree for the night, and in the morning they fly off in different directions. Parting comes for everyone, he says; this one, at least, has a purpose. Fourth, the last things. With his own sword the prince cuts off his long hair. A hunter in a dull-colored robe passes by, and the prince trades his fine silk clothes for that plain cloth. The poem says the hunter was a god in disguise. Then Chandaka turns for home, slowly, leading Kanthaka, and the poem says the horse licked the prince's feet and wept before he went. Since the old man on the cleared road, the poem has been taking things from the prince one at a time: his ease, a garden's charm, a friend's good argument, the palace. Today it's the jewels, his hair, his clothes and his last companion, and each one goes back with care.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give back one thing you don't need. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you're holding that isn't really yours to keep. A borrowed book. A coat that hasn't left the closet in years. A job on a committee you agreed to long ago. Pick one. Now picture giving it back the way the prince did: thanks first, then a clear word about why, then open hands. No slammed door. When you've pictured it, let your hands rest open in your lap for the rest of the sit. Later today, if it's a thing, give it back for real. The bell holds the time.
Chandaka sent back. At the forest's edge the prince thanks his attendant, answers his tears, and sends him home with the horse, the jewels and a message for the king. Today's word.
